explanation: Lafcadio Hearn used tsunami, Japanese for harbour wave, in an 1897 book about Japan. Teenager, at first spelled teen-ager, turns up only in the 1920s.

claims.text: 'Tsunami' was in English use by 1897, when Lafcadio Hearn used it in Gleanings in Buddha-Fields.
'Teenager' is first recorded in the 1920s, in the hyphenated form 'teen-ager'.
Japanese tsunami means 'harbour wave', from tsu, 'harbour', and nami, 'wave'.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: The earliest known print use of "teenager" is generally dated to 1913, though some sources date it later. [...] The Oxford English Dictionary's earliest evidence is from 1913, in the Every Evening Commercial of Wilmington, Delaware. [...] Merriam-Webster also gives 1913 as the first known use. [...] The Wikipedia article says the Wilmington paper printed it as two words, "Teen Ager," [...] Etymonline puts the noun at 1922 [...] Collins gives [1935–40; teenage + -er 1] as the word origin. [...] The 1913 date is the best-supported answer for the first known use.

claimResults.note: The OED and Merriam-Webster both date 'teenager' to 1913, printed as two words ('Teen Ager'); only Etymonline gives 1922. So 'first recorded in the 1920s, in the hyphenated form' is wrong as written, and so are the value 1922, the display 'the 1920s' and the explanation's 'turns up only in the 1920s'.

issues.note: Fixable: restate teenager as first recorded in 1913 (OED, Merriam-Webster). The key survives the fix: a second search ('tsunami earliest use in English Lafcadio Hearn 1897 Gleanings in Buddha-Fields Japanese harbour wave') found the OED, Merriam-Webster and Etymonline all dating tsunami to 1896, 17 years before 1913, so C17's ten-year gap still holds. That search tied Hearn's 1897 book to the word only through a Wikipedia reference-desk thread (Tier C), so the Hearn attribution in c1 and in the explanation needs its own Tier A or B source. Changed values and claims need two fresh checks (§9.7).
